moves.spoken: White plays d4, and Black replies with the bizarre g5 — the Borg, a reversed Grob.
White simply grabs on g5.
If Black takes the bishop, White takes on h5 with mate in two.
Black stops the mate, but White grabs another pawn — up two now, and dragging the king into the open.
The king is hauled out to e7 — what more could you ask from five moves?

Careful with the bishop — Black wants to take on d4, and if White recaptures with the queen, the bishop on h5 hangs. So the bishop to e3, adding a defender to d4 — now recapturing with a pawn deforms Black's camp.
Develop — but the knight to f3 would be a blunder. The knight to c3 is right, threatening the knight to c5, almost mate.

This bishop is a nuisance, so retreat it to e2. Sometimes a bishop on e2 is fine — not super active, but with two extra pawns and the black king stranded on e7, it is totally OK for a piece to sit on a quiet square, provided there is a good reason for it.
No reason not to trade — take, and keep developing with the knight to f3.
Which side to castle? Since Black no longer has those kingside pawns, castling short would hand him a ready-made attack — so White will castle long.
Ignore the knight on g4 — a knight there does not always do anything. But before castling long, get rid of it, or Black forks the pawn on f2.
So chase it — only to prepare castling, not because the knight is doing anything.
And remember — it matters less to ruin the pawn structure, more to wreck the structure around the king.
Taking on a6 would open the b-file and help Black attack — don't. The time has come to open the centre.
And do not push d5 — exactly what to avoid. Just take the pawn and open the d-file.
Black weakens a square with the recapture. Look for the tactic: the rook and queen sit in an x-ray, and with an x-ray you look for a discovery.
Move the knight and clear the d6-pawn and White wins the queen — the knight takes on e5 does both, and if Black recaptures, a check wins.
The queen check ends it — Black loses the queen and gets mated in the bargain.
There is even a mate in two: check first with the bishop to h5...
...then a piece to f7 blocks the king's escape, and the rook delivers mate.

g5 is terrible, and terrible after e4 too. Nothing extraordinary was needed — e4 prepared the mate, the bishop to e2 threatened to take on h5 with mate, and the key move to notice was dropping the bishop back: it had done its job, so retreat it and keep developing. No crazy g4 — just develop, and castle long to deny any attack.
